title: TB6-00147

Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The Principal Appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX (XXXX), and the Minor Appellants, XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX, are citizens of Somalia and appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated December 9, 2015, rejecting their claims for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The Principal Appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX (XXXX), and the Minor Appellants, XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX, are citizens of Somalia and appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated December 9, 2015, rejecting their claims for refugee protection. The Principal Appellant was appointed the designated representative of the Minor Appellants. The Appellants are not submitting new evidence and are not requesting a hearing. The Appellants ask that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) set aside the decision of the RPD and find that the Appellants are either Convention refugees or persons in need of protection, or that the RAD refer the matter back to the RPD for reconsideration.

Pursuant to section 111(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD sets aside the determination of the RPD and substitutes its determination that the Appellants are Convention refugees.

The Appellants are mother and daughters. XXXX alleges that she and her husband ran a XXXX in their home in Mogadishu XXXX both boys and girls. She alleges that on XXXX XXXX, 2015, while she was out with her daughters, Al Shabab came to her home and shot and killed her sister. Her husband manage to escape. XXXX family made their way to Nairobi, sold their family home in Somalia, and with the proceeds of the sale the Appellants came to Canada using false Australian passports. They filed their refugee claim on August of 2015.

The RPD rendered its decision December 9, 2015 rejects the Appellants' refugee claim. With a decision dated March 22, 2016 the RAD confirmed the decision of the RPD. The Appellants appealed the RAD's decision to the Federal Court. By decision dated XXXX XXXX, 2016, the Federal Court allowed the Appeal and returned the matter to the RAD.

For questions of fact, mixed fact and law, and law, the RAD has applied the standard of correctness as per Huruglica.1 In assessing issues involving credibility of oral testimony, the RAD may apply the RAD's modified standard of reasonableness in those situations where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in making findings of credibility as per the decision in X (Re).2
Accordingly, the RAD will conduct its own analysis of the Record to determine if the RPD erred.

The RPD found that the Appellants had not proven their identity as citizens of Somalia and that they were not credible witnesses with respect to their allegations against Al Shabab. The Appellants submit that the RPD erred in its conclusion with respect to the Appellants' identity as citizens of Somalia and in its credibility assessment.
paragraphs.heading_before: ANALYSIS ON THE MERITS OF THE APPEAL

paragraphs.text: The Appellants presented no identity documents at the RPD. However, the RPD did note that the documentary evidence with respect to Somalia indicates that the country does not have a functioning government and that its citizens have not been able to obtain identity documents. In support of their identity, the Appellants produced an affidavit from XXXX husband, documentation with respect to the transfer of funds of the sale of their property in Somalia, and a witness who provided oral testimony at the RPD hearing.

With respect to XXXX husband's affidavit, the RPD had concerns with respect to the allegations against Al Shahab. However, the fact that the author of the document was the Principal Appellant's husband was not challenged by the RPD.

With respect to the document concerning the sale of the house in Somalia, the RPD gave the document no weight since there was no original and it had no way of verifying its authenticity. The Appellant submits that the RPD has erred in declining to give the affidavit of the sale any weight because its authenticity could not be verified. The Appellant submits that the affidavit was sworn before a notary and that there was no evidence that the affidavit was suspect. The Appellant submits that the RPD cannot discount the document simply because it is a copy and the original was available.

The RAD concurs that a document cannot be denied evidentiary weight simply because it is not an original. The RPD provided no reason to discount the document other than because it was a copy and the RPD could not determine its authenticity. The RPD did not indicate any specific concern with any aspect of the document and therefore erred in giving the affidavit of sale no weight.

The Appellant provided a witness to corroborate her identity. The Appellant testified that the witness and his family lived directly across from her home in Mogadishu and that they had last seen each other in Somalia in 2009. The RPD, however, found the witness' testimony lacking in credibility and assigned it no weight.

Specifically, the RPD had concerns with the following elements of the witness' testimony: a) The Appellant testified that her family had abandoned their home in Mogadishu in 1991 and fled to XXXX where they remained until 1997. The witness, however, testified that they had been away for only one year. b) The Appellant testified that her father had been killed in 1991, but the witness initially said that he had been killed in 2015 and then later changed his testimony and said that the Appellant's father had been killed in 1991. c) Neither the Appellant nor the witness could specify the first or second time they met in Canada, even though the meetings had been only in the last couple of months before the hearing.

The Appellant submits that both the Appellant and the witness were under 10 years of age when she and her family left and subsequently returned to their home, and that it is unreasonable for the RPD to impugn the witness' credibility simply because he could not remember when the Appellant had left and then returned to Mogadishu.

The Appellant also notes that after the witness initially erred as to the date her father was killed, he corrected himself without it being brought to his attention. With respect to the dates they met after they were in Canada, the Appellant submits that a close reading of the transcript3 indicates the both she and the witness were consistent regarding the second, third, and fourth visits - which is sufficient in this regard.
The Appellant further submits that the witness was broadly consistent about everything except for when she and her family fled Mogadishu between 1991 and 1997, which is some twenty years ago.

The RAD notes that the witness was able to recall generally when the Appellant and her family had gone away, but could not remember for how long. The witness was also able to recall that the Appellant's father had been killed, and eventually when he was killed - later correcting himself and providing the right date (1991). Both the witness and the Appellant were consistent with respect to the occupations of the witness' parents. The RAD also acknowledges that during the period 1991-1997 when both the Appellant and the witness left Mogadishu, there was a great deal of chaos in the country and that both were quite young. It would therefore be unreasonable to expect them to remember exact dates. The RAD therefore accepts the testimony of the witness.
The RAD concludes that, given the documentary evidence produced by the Appellants and the oral testimony of the witness, the Appellants are citizens of Somalia.

In allowing the appeal, the Federal Court stated: ...the Applicants should also have been assessed as being a mother and two young daughters who fall under risk profiles identified by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees in January 2014 as applying to those fleeing Southern and Central Somalia. They come within the risk profiles of "women and girls", "children" and "members of a minority clan". As established by Madam Justice Dawson, as she then was, in Pastrana Viafm·a v Canada (-Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2006 FC 1526 at paragraph 6: ''the Board must consider all of the grounds for making a claim to refugee status, even if the grounds are not raised during a hearing by a claimant." Before the RPD, the Applicants' counsel argued that Applicants were Convention refugees based, if nothing else, solely on their gender and membership in a minority clan. The Applicants have always maintained that they are at risk in Somalia by virtue of their immutable characteristics and on the basis independent country condition reports regardless of whether they have a personalized fear of Al-Shabaab. The RAD only chose to address the finding that the fear of Al-Shabaab was not proven. Had identity been accepted, this error alone would have been fatal to the Decision. As the RAD's decision on identity is unreasonable, the entire Decision must therefore be set aside.

Based on this statement, the Appellants submit that: "Even if the credibility issue regarding the husband's affidavit (i.e. shop versus school) is maintained by the RAD, the Appellants are members of a minority clan, are 'women and girls' and two of them are girls."4

The RAD acknowledges that the documentary evidence indicates that women and girls are at high risk in Somalia by virtue of their gender. In particular, the RAD notes the UNHCR's report of 20145 UNHCR considers that persons with any of the profiles below, or a combination thereof, may be in need of international protection in the sense of the Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees ("1951 Convention"). Where relevant, particular consideration needs to be given to any past persecution to which applicants for refugee status may have been subjected. In light of the history of violent conflict and human rights abuses in Somalia, the applicability of the exclusion clauses may need to be considered in certain cases. The profiles listed here are not necessarily exhaustive; they are based on information available to UNHCR at the time of writing. Hence, a claim should not automatically be considered as without merit simply because it does not fall within any of the profiles identified here. In the forthcoming eligibility guidelines these profiles will be further updated as needed and analyzed in detail. (emphasis added) Potential Risk Profiles: 8. Women and girls; 9. Children;

The Federal Court, in relying on the Federal Court of Appeal decision in Adjei6 stated "This Court has consistently said that such individuals are entitled to protection if they prove that their subjective fear of persecution is objectively affirmed by showing that persecution is a real risk if their identity becomes known".7 Given the objective evidence, the RAD finds that the Appellants need Canada's protection.
Pursuant to Section 111(1)(b) of the IRPA, the RAD sets aside the determination of the RPD and substitutes its determination that the Appellants are Convention refugees.

The Appeal is allowed. (signed) "Pasquale Fiorino" Pasquale Fiorino September 1, 2017 Date 1 M.C.I. v. Huruglica, Bujar (F.C.A., no.
